claim: People given the 2-4-6 task mostly test triples that fit their own hypothesis; only 6 of 29 (Wason 1960) announced the right rule first time, 21 of 29 eventually; more disconfirming tests (I:C 1.79 vs 0.24) went with earlier success. Replicated across many rule-discovery studies. (Wason 1960 original opened in gap pass: 6 of 29 first-try, 13 one wrong, 9 two or more, 1 none; index 1.79 n=6 vs 0.24 n=22, p=0.0002.)
agent_test: Log share of tests outside the current hypothesis per episode on a 2-4-6 style task and correlate with success.
audit_note: The 21/29 eventual-solver figure is not stated in Wason's original text (it gives 6 first-time, 13 one-wrong, 9 two-plus, 1 none) and comes from Jhaveri et al.; 'replicated across many studies' is from Klayman and Ha's review.

claim: Positive testing is a general heuristic, not irrational by itself: a positive test can falsify a hypothesis when the hypothesis is broader than, overlaps, or is disjoint from the true rule, but it can never falsify when the hypothesis is a strict subset (narrower) of the true rule, where only negative tests can. Whether a test is informative depends on that set relation.
agent_test: Tag each test with H vs target relation; check that failure concentrates in narrower-than-target cases.
audit_note: Klayman and Ha show positive tests can also falsify when the hypothesized set merely overlaps or is disjoint from the true rule, not only when it is broader; positive tests fail only when the hypothesis is a strict subset of the rule.
claim_before_audit: Positive testing is a general heuristic, not irrational by itself: it can falsify only when the hypothesis is broader than the true rule, and cannot when it is narrower. Whether a test is informative depends on that set relation.

claim: Explicit instruction to seek disconfirming cases, or to treat the task as two complementary hypotheses (DAX/MED), raises human success on 2-4-6 from about 20% to 40-60% or more. Gale and Ball found goal count mattered, not labels.
agent_test: Add a 'name two complementary hypotheses and test both' step; compare success at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: Branchini control baseline was 36.7% not 20%; 20% baseline comes from Gale and Ball; Gorman abstract gives no rates.

claim: A short think-in-opposites training took human 2-4-6 success from 36.66% to 78.33% (N=120 in 2023; N=180 in 2025, properties-only arm 38.33%). The opposites step is the active part. CAUTION: the control and opposites percentages are identical in both papers (47/60 and 22/60) and may share data.
agent_test: Compare 'list properties of last test' vs 'test its opposite' prompts on an LLM at equal tokens.

claim: On the abstract Wason selection task fewer than 10% choose p and not-q; content (deontic rules) helps humans and LLMs; matching bias and rarity-based information gain explain much of it, so low scores are not simply a failure to falsify.
agent_test: Not needed for the agent; use deontic vs abstract variants only as a sanity probe.
audit_note: Minor: Lampinen/Dasgupta paper first author is Dasgupta; Wikipedia gives <10% for full correct solution only.

claim: Confirmation preference in humans loads on one general factor across three paradigms (N=200): confirming options 69.1% vs disconfirming 48.2%, d=0.89; search effect d=1.18, weighing d=0.31.
agent_test: Not directly testable on the agent; informs that search, not weighing, is the main gap.

claim: LLMs are poor at 2-4-6 style hypothesis testing: WILT best 14/50 (28%) in 2024; Numberwang pilot mean 11% of rules; Failing-to-Falsify 6% to 78% across 11 models; FalsifyBench 12% to 75% across 12 models. Failure often includes confirmatory testing even when told not to.
agent_test: Run the agent on WILT-style and FalsifyBench-style games against plain, at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: 14/50 not on WILT abstract but 28% is; Numberwang 11% mean confirmed on blog (informal pilot). Sources are distinct papers/blog.

claim: Across LLMs, the share of tests that fit the current hypothesis predicts failure: FalsifyBench Spearman rho -0.779 (success) and -0.937 (conclusive falsification), mixed model coefficient -4.15; Failing-to-Falsify finds a positive link between I:C and success (Spearman about 0.75 thinking, 0.54 non-thinking). Both are observational.
agent_test: Measure the negative-test share inside the agent's S4 and use it as a diagnostic.
audit_note: Minor: FalsifyBench -0.779, -0.937, -4.15 verified; Failing-to-Falsify Spearman 0.75/0.54 are read from figure labels, not found in text (text says significant positive, stronger for thinking).

claim: Reasoning ('thinking') models do better but not clearly by testing more incompatibly: FalsifyBench says reasoning models test outside their hypothesis much more, while Failing-to-Falsify reports thinking raises success without consistently raising I:C (Qwen3-8B 0.06 to 0.21). Gap pass: within each mode Think-in-Opposites raised success in 11 of 11 cells while I:C fell in 4 of 22 interventions (e.g. GPT-4o 0.25 to 0.17 with success 0.11 to 0.16), so I:C is not the whole mechanism; no mediation or token-matched test exists.
agent_test: Compare I:C of thinking vs non-thinking mode on the same model across both task designs.

claim: A prompt that forces a test of the opposite of the last test (Think-in-Opposites) raises LLM success for thinking models (Qwen3-32B 0.41 to 0.61; Gemini-2.5-Pro 0.73 to about 0.78) but not reliably for non-thinking ones (Dual-Goal cut Qwen3-32B non-thinking to 0.10). Average discovery 42% to 56%.
agent_test: Add a forced-opposite test turn in S4 only when reasoning is on; compare on Blicket and 2-4-6 variants.

claim: Fine-tuning on Think-in-Opposites traces raises success (8B 0.21 to 0.35; 32B 0.41 to 0.64; 8B from 32B teacher 0.59) and partly transfers to Blicket (32B 0.57 to 0.77, below prompt 0.86). Not applicable to our no-training agent except as evidence the habit is learnable.
agent_test: None at equal tokens (training); the prompt version is K10.

claim: Confirmation bias is not the whole failure: oracle quality does not explain success (oracle error OR 0.885, interval spans zero), and failed games have more hypotheses that only partly overlap or miss the target; WILT o1-preview used 9 tests, 5 confirming, leaving most budget unused.
agent_test: Log hypothesis-target overlap per turn; test a rule 'do not stop early, spend budget on distinct tests'.

claim: LLMs that can solve a problem are far worse at refuting a wrong solution: REFUTE best model breaks under 9% of subtly wrong solutions while able to solve about 48.7% from scratch; having the correct solution gives only 3%. In Zendo, an LLM experiment proposer did no better than a random proposer. Gap pass: the 3% is the share of extra submissions broken when the correct solution was given, and execution feedback (ReAct) gave 6.8-8.6% for o3-mini, no real gain; a random-input generator that never sees the bad code broke 14% of 403 candidate problems, which were removed from the benchmark by design.
agent_test: Give the agent a wrong candidate and ask for a breaking input; score vs random-input baseline at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: 48.7% is in Table 1 (abstract says up to 48%); the 3% is share of new submissions invalidated, as the claim's gap note says.

claim: Falsification-built agents with statistical control work: POPPER keeps Type-I error near 0.1 where baselines reach 0.145-0.311, with 66.5% more power than ReAct (DiscoveryBench) and 3.17x Self-Refine (TargetVal-IL2); matched 9 experts at 9.7x speed. Main failures are misread p-values (35.9%) and weak test design (28.1%), not hallucination. Needs data and valid p-values.
agent_test: Apply sequential e-value style stopping only where numeric tests exist; otherwise skip.

claim: A related benchmark, P-Bench, shows strong agents still make inferential errors on hypothesis tests (hard strict pass@1: GPT-5.4 30.5%); RL with statistical reward lifted a 14B model to 33.0%. Read from a Hugging Face page; weakly verified.
agent_test: Not testable for us.

claim: Sycophantic or hypothesis-sampled evidence stops discovery: in a preregistered 2-4-6 variant (N=557, 504 analysed), default GPT-5.1 examples gave 5.9% discovery vs 29.5% for random sequences, and raised confidence. Cells re-read: Rule Confirming 8.4%, Agreeable 11.8%, Rule Disconfirming 14.1%; confidence change +5.4 default, -56.8 random; chatbot was GPT-5.1-Chat; humans wrote the hypotheses.
agent_test: Check that candidate-test generation is not sampled from the candidate's own hypothesis; use code-generated mutated inputs.

claim: Self-correction without external feedback does not improve reasoning and can hurt (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5 75.8 to 41.8). Asking a model to critique its own answer is not a severe test.
agent_test: Already in schema: tests must be code or held-out. Compare model self-critique to code check at equal tokens.

claim: Philosophically, falsification is never fully mechanical: Popper says acceptance of basic statements rests on a decision or agreement (like a jury verdict); a failed prediction does not show which assumption is at fault (Putnam; Lakatos's protective belt); and Miller and Tichy showed in 1974 that Popper's definition of verisimilitude is formally defective for false theories, which Popper partly conceded. Oaksford and Chater (1994) state that philosophers regarded strict falsificationism as unworkable.
agent_test: Add a step that, after a failed test, lists which assumption failed (candidate, test, or setup) before discarding.
audit_note: SEP says Miller and Tichy showed in 1974 that Popper's verisimilitude definition is formally defective for false theories and Popper conceded the mistake but kept the concept as heuristic; Duhem-Quine is not named (Putnam and Lakatos are); the 'philosophers judged unworkable' line is not in the SEP pages; a03-a06 are all one SEP entry.
claim_before_audit: Philosophically, falsification is never mechanical: basic statements are accepted by decision (a03), a failed prediction does not locate the faulty assumption (Duhem-Quine; Lakatos), and Popper's verisimilitude was refuted in 1974 (Miller, Tichy). Philosophers judged strict falsificationism unworkable.

claim: Pre-committed severe tests change outcomes: Registered Reports in psychology had 44% positive first hypotheses vs 96% in standard papers (N=71 vs 152). Mayo's severity rule: a pass counts only if flaws would likely have been detected.
agent_test: Fix the test before seeing the candidate answer; compare pass rate of pre-registered vs post-hoc tests.
audit_note: Neither listed source (Mayo abstracts, SEP Popper) contains the 44% vs 96% Registered Reports figures; they come from Scheel et al. (2021), which I confirmed (71 vs 152) but which is not in the evidence; Mayo PDF text was unreadable; 'change outcomes' is a causal reading of a between-paper-type comparison.

claim: Autonomous science systems claim to use falsification (Baby-AIGS FalsificationAgent, AI co-scientist reflection) but report weak quantitative evidence for the falsification part itself; expert ratings of falsification were below conference level.
agent_test: Not testable directly; treat as unproven.

claim: Tests written after seeing the candidate code inherit its faults: fault detection about 14% when an LLM writes tests after its own faulty code in the same session vs about 25% from a fresh session given only the task text (5 LLMs, 3 coding benchmarks); an earlier study found test bug detection 47% worse on real-world incorrect code and 11 models make worse tests for wrong code.
agent_test: Compare checks written with and without sight of the candidate on planted-bug tasks; report detection rate.

claim: LLMs are poor at blaming the right artifact when evidence conflicts: across 7 LLMs and 3,192 Java instances they detect doc faults at 67-94% but implementation-only faults 21-43 points less, rank sources by reliability near chance for code faults (tau_b <= 0.10), and confidence rarely separates right from wrong. No study tests Duhem-Quine blame between candidate, test and auxiliary assumption directly.
agent_test: After a failed test, inject faults into either the test or the candidate and score how often the agent blames the right one.

claim: Passing LLM-written tests is weak evidence of correctness: planted-flaw detection by LLM-generated tests is low (SWE-Mutation: 7 LLMs, 2,636 mutants, verification 8-40%, detection 25-72%, agentic mutants drop mean detection 71.04% to 39.81%; Hamidi et al. 2026: over 6,000 faulty programs, detection often near zero). This is the nearest measured version of Mayo severity.
agent_test: Plant known flaws in agent answers and score the share the S4 step catches; use that as the severity number.
audit_note: Minor: SWE-Mutation was read from a benchmark-list summary page, not the paper; the Mayo-severity link is the researcher's interpretation.

claim: Feedback on one's own tests helps people switch from confirming to counterexample choices: selection-task meta-analysis of 228 experiments finds that repeated tasks with feedback shift choices to counterexamples and that framing and instructions help; 99 experiments show dependent, redundant selections.
agent_test: Show the agent the result of its last test before it picks the next; compare with no feedback.

claim: The gap between solving and falsifying has not closed with the 2026 model generation on the one benchmark that tests it: FalsifyBench top score 75% (GPT-5.2-Chat), others 12-68%, 12 models, 100 games; no Claude or Gemini frontier model was in the list.
agent_test: Run the same games on our target model and log positive-test share.

claim: No paper yet measures a forced opposite-test step against best-of-N at equal tokens on answer-checking tasks (open gap 1); evidence is limited to 2-4-6 style games, REFUTE and POPPER. Branchini replication by a third lab (gap 3) and the Klayman and Ha set-relation question for LLMs (gap 10) also found no new study.
agent_test: Run opposite-test vs best-of-N at equal tokens on a code-checking task.
